https://www.newsday.com/entertainment/tv.text: Peter Lassally, pictured here in 2007, left an indelible mark on late-night TV. Credit: Getty Images for AFI/Mark Mainz By Verne Gay verne.gay@newsday.com @vernejgay Updated July 23, 2026 4:40 pm Share Peter Lassally, who produced Johnny Carson's "Tonight Show" for nearly a quarter century and masterminded David Letterman's move from NBC to CBS, certainly led a remarkable life. There were, however, no guarantees that Lassally — who died earlier this week at the age of 93 — would actually survive to live out the one he did. Around the age of 10, in 1943, he was sent to Theresienstadt in Czechoslovakia, along with his mother and sister. "A strange place," he once elliptically recalled, while the Holocaust Encyclopedia elaborated: In preparation for a 1944 visit by the Red Cross, "German authorities ordered the beautification" of the death camp, but to make it "appear less crowded" also sent 7,500 inmates to Auschwitz. "You never knew if the next time you were called out, it might be to board another transport," he said in an interview with Dennis Carlyle Darling, author of a 2023 history, "Borrowed Time: Survivors of Nazi Terezín Remember" ("Terezin" was the camp's Czech name.) Theresienstadt was liberated in 1945. By 1947, Lassally was living in New York. By 1951, he was an usher, along with lifelong friend Regis Philbin, at Radio City Music Hall, then at 30 Rock. By around 1958, he was president of Arthur Godfrey's production company. By 1972, he was producer of "Tonight." By 1993, he had launched a late night show on CBS. Only in America, as the saying goes. Lassally was one of a small group of people who effectively created the golden years of late night TV. Some are natural-born showmen who knew how to shape talent (Lorne Michaels). Some knew how to coddle that talent (NBC's Dave Tebet). Some were enforcers (Jay Leno's longtime producer Helen Kushnick.) Sign up for Newsday's Entertainment newsletter Get the latest on celebs, TV and more. By clicking Sign up, you agree to our privacy policy . What (or who) then was Lassally? Among the many hosts he mentored over the years, Garry Shandling once explained that "one of Peter's real strengths is getting the host to understand how to listen, how to ask the questions that an audience might want to hear, and to listen to the answer and to not be thinking ahead with the joke." Shandling's alter ego on "The Larry Sanders Show" (1986-90) of course pointedly ignored all of this. What Lasally had in abundance was advice, counsel and wisdom, to be dismissed at one's own peril. Few ever did. Lassally was centered in an uncentered TV world, where ego, narcissism and insecurity ruled, while talent scrambled for a footing, or for survival. Could Carson have thrived all those years without Lassally by his side, or could Letterman? We'll never know although (in fact) we probably do. Admirers called him the "host whisperer," as if he were some sort of oracle with a mystical hold as opposed to a producer who needed to get the show on every night. HIs speaking style was sotto voce: Quiet, unadorned, direct. You leaned in to listen, the words freighted with significance, and a sense that the man speaking them understood life-and-death stakes — and that show business was hardly life-and-death. He had some stumbles. When Shandling exited as "Tonight Show" guest host, he was left with the other guest host, his friend Joan Rivers. She later claimed, falsely, that Lassally had agreed to produce her late-night Fox show. That led to a breach with Rivers, and nearly with Carson. After the triumph with Letterman, he had hoped to groom his successor — Craig Ferguson, who hosted the 12:30 show — and when CBS chose Stephen Colbert instead, he finally retired, his disappointment palpable. By then, this Carson confidant, this Letterman anchor, the death camp survivor who had witnessed the worst of humanity, had changed late night TV forever and for the better anyway. He hardly ever talked about the deep past because "I learned to block out all the ugly things," he told Darling. "I want to move forward, not return to the past." In a statement, his family said, "Peter built a life defined not by the horrors he endured as a child but by resilience, generosity, curiosity and optimism." Indeed, the host whisperer's ultimate triumph. By Verne Gay verne.gay@newsday.com @vernejgay Verne Gay is Newsday's TV writer and critic. He has covered the media business for more than 30 years. http://www.bignewsnetwork.com/news/27921.text: Big News Network.com MAGA influencer who denied Ukraine has neo-Nazis interviews one Laura Loomer met with Andrey Biletsky, the Ukrainian ultranationalist and former commander of the far-right Azov Battalion American influencer Laura Loomer is currently on aPR tourof Ukraine, which she insists doesn't have a neo-Nazi problem. Disproving her own point, she has interviewed the far-right activist and commander of the notorious Azov battalion, Andrey 'White Leader' Biletsky. Loomer, who has cultivated close ties to US President Donald Trump's MAGA movement, claimed on Tuesday that she had met Biletsky in his home city of Kharkov and would publish an extended interview with him. Biletsky, a prominent Ukrainian far-right figure since the 2000s, helped establish the ultranationalist Social-National Assembly, which has widely been described as a neo-Nazi, white supremacist organization. He later rose to national prominence as commander of the Azov Battalion, which began as a far-right volunteer militia before being incorporated into Ukraine's security forces following the Western-backed armed coup in Kiev in 2014. Biletsky now holds the rank of brigadier general and commands the 3rd Army Corps, one of the formations that emerged from the wider Azov movement. Since the escalation of the conflict with Russia in 2022, Azov-linked groups have undertaken extensive efforts to whitewash themselves, denying their extremist origins. This publicity drive has had its roadbumps. In 2024, the 3rd Army Corps had to cancel a charm offensive in Europe after some of its members sparked outrage with aphoto opat the Auschwitz memorial in Poland, where one soldier posed in a T-shirt featuring the metal band M8l8th, whose name means "Hitler's Hammer." Before 2022, US assistance to Azov was banned over concerns about the unit's ideology and reported abuses, while Russia has designated it as a terrorist group. During her trip, Loomer also interviewed Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky and accepted his assurances that the country does not have a neo-Nazi problem. She additionally met Yevgeny Khmara, who has been named as a potential replacement defense minister, and former Prime Minister Andrey Yatsenyuk. The influencer also visited a facility operated by DTEK, the private energy company owned by UkrainianoligarchRinat Akhmetov. In an on-brand remark, Loomer said it was "refreshing" that she hasn't "seen a single Muslim here." Ukraine in reality has a significant Muslim minority, which includes Akhmetov and some other influential figures, such as former Defense Minister Rustem Umerov. Loomer's enthusiastic praise for Ukraine and its leadership stands in sharp contrast to her earlier criticism of Kiev, prompting accusations that she is shilling for the Zelensky government. She has said the trip changed her view of the country and denied that it was financed by Kiev, claiming she paid for it herself with support from "private Americans" concerned about her security. https://www.countrylife.co.uk/travel/wel.text: Exquisite houses, the beauty of Nature, and how to get the most from your life, straight to your inbox. You are now subscribed Your newsletter sign-up was successful The spa at Raffles at The OWO is London's first Guerlain-branded destination spa. (Image credit: Raffles) Share Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Pinterest Share this article Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter The Spa at Mandarin Oriental Hyde Park All too often, Londoners overlook the Mandarin Oriental which looms grandly over Hyde Park’s southern flank. However, the food I had at Dinner by Heston London, on the hotel’s ground floor, is one of the best meals I’ve had in my 15 years living here, and I adore the subtle leaf motifs scattered throughout the interiors whose shapes were directly inspired by the park’s trees. The serene cream and dark wood spa marries old-school five-star service with Eastern influences to great effect. They currently partner with British brand OSKIA and the signature facial combines facial massage, acupressure work, LED therapy and hot compresses to erase any unnecessary contours. It’s a fantastic non-invasive, all-rounder treatment and while some visitors might not appreciate the warren of subterranean rooms, corridors and facilities, I think it’s an easy way to find some respite from the hectic city one floor above. Pfeffer Sal (Image credit: Pfeffer Sal) A hidden gem — quite literally, it's hidden at the bottom of a mews street — Pfeffer Sal , takes an individual approach to every client. Latest Videos From Country Life Watch full video here: It's a particularly good option for facial newbies and brides who want great results without all of the postulating that's sadly part and parcel of the wellness world. Start with the The Three Sixty complete with skin consultation and skin imaging technology — before advancing to a course of treatment. The team take customer's health seriously, going as far to install a NASA-specification air purification and filtration system. London grime doesn't stand a chance. Surrenne Belgravia Surrenne connects The Emory and Berkley hotels, but operates more along the lines of a private members’ wellness club. Facilities include a 22-metre-long lap pool, sauna, steam room, snow shower, gym, hammams and treatment rooms. Sign up for the Country Life Newsletter Exquisite houses, the beauty of Nature, and how to get the most from your life, straight to your inbox. Membership includes perks such as hyperbaric sessions and Tracy Anderson classes in the UK’s only dedicated Tracy Anderson studio. (Anderson innovated a dance-inspired fitness programme beloved by Gwyneth Paltrow and Victoria Beckham. When I attempted it, I thought I was going into cardiac arrest.) The massages are my favourite part of their offering. If you don’t quite know what you want opt for the I NEED IT ALL and your therapist will curate an hour-long treatment made up of lots of different approaches, from deep tissue to Ayurveda. The RECOVERY RITUAL is fantastic if you’ve made it through a Tracy Anderson class intact because it incorporates magnesium which can ease delayed-onset muscle soreness and regulate sleep. Dr Barbara Sturm (Image credit: Dr Barbara Sturm) World-renowned skincare expert Barbara Sturm made her long-awaited UK debut five years ago with a boutique and spa on Mayfair’s Mount Street. The ground floor is a sweet shop for grown-ups: row upon row of pristine white bottles lining the walls, a mirrored sink and a green marble ‘discovery’ table, stacked high with the brand’s popular Molecular Cosmetics range. There are two express treatment rooms — perfect for a quick lunchtime pick-me-up — and four fully-fitted ones, spread across the aforementioned ground and lower ground floor. As well as the signature Barbara Sturm glow facial, customers can book in for high-tech anti-ageing and body treatments. There’s little reason to deviate from the former, however: an hour of intense facial massage, cleansers, masks and serums that will leave your face feeling brighter and tighter for days afterwards. There’s also the option to add microneedling or microdermabrasion. Guerlain Spa at Raffles at The OWO The Guerlain Spa at The OWO — which comprises a 20-metre indoor pool, vitality pool, nine treatment rooms, sauna, steam room, state-of-the-art gym and experience showers — is ecclesiastical in scale. There aren’t many hotels in this central of a location (Whitehall) that can boast enough space to give away 2,500 square metres to wellness. The pool has double-height ceilings. The plush treatment beds are so thick they verge on mattresses. The impressive array of treatments includes reflexology with Andrea Hurst who has been practicing for more than 30 years. Extremely passionate about her craft, she maintains long-standing relationships with the majority of her clients, getting to know their lives, families and innermost thoughts. Sessions are part reflexology and part therapy — and part steep learning experience. During mine, I learned that in holistic therapies, the right side of the body and foot is traditionally associated with the masculine, and the left with the feminine. Melanie Grant (Image credit: Melanie Grant) There are facialists and then there is Melanie Grant , whose much-lauded expertise has arrived at her debut UK clinic on Mount Street in Mayfair. Her reputation is built on treatments combining high-grade technology, innovative formulations and ‘old-school’ techniques, addressing issues from congested complexions and sun-damage to remodelling the skin’s layers from deep within. I could talk you through the Ultimate Collagen Treatment + Exosome Infusion (stellar for rejuvenation), but no treatment is a set script. ‘Each is built around the skin in front of us on the day, taking into account lifestyle, hormones, seasons, travel and stress,' Grant tells me. 'We are never wedded to a single method or device, but we’re focused on a signature outcome — a healthy, resilient complexion.’ Biome by Corinthia London Biome is perhaps London’s most surprising spa because its holistic focus and deeply nurturing atmosphere is so at odds with the very elegant and formal hotel that houses it. They recently partnered with Wildsmith — a Hampshire-based brand from the brains behind biodynamic farm and hotel Heckfield Place (who, incidentally, have their own fantastic Bothy spa). Today, Heckfield is home to the UK’s only biodynamic tree nursery where pioneering horticulturist Wiliam Walker Wildsmith’s ancient trees are propagated for future generations. There’s an entire facial menu to choose from, but go for the Radical Botany: magic medicine for skin dulled by urban pollution. My favourite bit is when the therapist applies light and sustained pressure to certain points on the head and spine (craniosacral holds to give the action its proper name). The space itself is a masterclass in urban spa design: the textured walls, rounded treatment pods and brilliantly-thought-out lighting completely distract from the fact that there aren’t any windows. You could easily while away a day here (there’s a heat and water circuit, gym, hair salon and sauna). Omorovicza (Image credit: Omorovicza) Omorovicza's Andrassy facial is a marvel for sad-looking skin. Therapists use vigorous massage techniques — borrowed from Hungarian wellness practices — alongside Omorovicza’s gorgeous products (my longstanding favourite is Queen Essence) to lift, sculpt and treat. The setting surely helps, too. You’ll find its standalone Londonstore on Mayfair’s South Audley Street — think blush-pink brick flooring with matching daubed walls and gently vaulted treatment rooms that all act to cocoon you instantly. The company has a BodySerum that uses sustainably sourced Icelandic microalgaeto target loss of elasticity and is brilliant for toning limbs — ready for those last-minute trips abroad. TOPICS Rosie Paterson Rosie is Country Life's Digital Content Director & Travel Editor. She joined the team in July 2014 — following a brief stint in the art world. In 2022, she edited the magazine's special Queen's Platinum Jubilee issue and coordinated Country Life's own 125 birthday celebrations. She has also been invited to judge a travel media award and chaired live discussions on the London property market, sustainability and luxury travel trends. Rosie studied Art History at university and, beyond Country Life, has written for Mr & Mrs Smith and The Gentleman's Journal, among others. The rest of the office likes to joke that she splits her time between Claridge’s, Devon and the Maldives. https://www.politico.eu/article/jordan-b.text: PARIS — French presidential candidates from the far left to the far right are blasting the memorandum of understanding on stopping migration across the English Channel that National Rally President Jordan Bardella signed with Reform U.K.’s Nigel Farage on Friday. Critics of the deal, which says in English that France “will ordinarily accept” migrants intercepted in the English Channel and sent back to French shores, accused the far-right MEP of attempting to cede French sovereignty on immigration matters. The pact only goes into effect if Reform UK and the National Rally take power in the United Kingdom and France, respectively. On X , Xavier Bertrand, the conservative president of the Hauts-de-France region that includes some of the most well-known launch points for the so-called “small boats” trying to reach the U.K. from France, accused Bardella of “bowing down” to Farage and wanting to make France the U.K.’s “subcontractor” on border enforcement. Advertisement Advertisement Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leading left-wing candidate for next year’s election, also said Bardella would turn France into a “gatekeeper” for the U.K. “This wasn’t France speaking, it was a fascist with no reputation and no standing,” he added during a campaign rally on Saturday. Gabriel Attal, the leader of President Emmanuel Macron’s Renaissance party, said Bardella “either doesn’t understand English, or is shockingly weak when it comes to defending French interests.” Edouard Philippe, the leading center-right candidate in the race, also mocked the Bardella-Farage agreement. “We didn’t see that one coming,” he said on X . Even the National Rally’s competitors on the far right called out the accord. “Jordan Bardella agrees to take in foreigners on our soil whom Great Britain does not want,” said Eric Zemmour , the leader of the anti-immigrant party Reconquest. “Having allies must NEVER come at any price — especially not at the expense of the integrity of our borders and our people.” Advertisement Advertisement Noticeably silent was National Rally presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen. The French far-right duo has struggled to find its footing since a court in July shortened Le Pen’s sentence for embezzlement of EU funds, allowing her to run. Bardella had previously been expected to be the party’s candidate in next year’s election. Last month, Farage announced that, if elected, he would launch the “largest military operation in the English Channel since World War II” to intercept small boats and return migrants to French shores. But a person close to Le Pen, speaking to POLITICO on condition of anonymity, raised doubts about the plan. “Why [send them back] to France if they aren’t French?” said the individual. Sarah Paillou contributed to this report.

https://www.standardspeaker.com/2026/08/.text: Dr. Peter Scirmantas accepts a medal from Lithuania’s Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys in Vilnius in July. SUBMITTED PHOTO By Ron Devlin | rdevlin@republicanherald.com | Republican Herald PUBLISHED: August 29, 2026 at 12:00 PM EDT | UPDATED: September 1, 2026 at 1:27 PM EDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... SHENANDOAH — The memory of his wife’s passing was still fresh when Dr. Peter Skirmantas went to Lithuania in July to accept a medal for her role in establishing the Lithuanian Heritage Museum. Anne Chaikowsky LaVoie Skirmantas died in March, four months before the Lithuanian government formally recognized her efforts. A rush of emotion flowed through Skirmantas as Kestutis Budrys, Lithuania’s foreign minister, presented him with the “Merits of Lithuanians Worldwide Award.” “I was trying not to weep,” confided Skirmantas, 75, a retired history professor. “I wished Anne had lived to get the award.” The award, one of the highest given to people in the Lithuanian diaspora, came three months after Archbishop Lionginas Virbilas visited the heritage museum in Shenandoah, officially designated “Little Lithuania” by the Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission. Based in Vilnius, Lithuania’s capital city, Virbilas ministers to Lithuanians worldwide. The archbishop spent a good deal of time in the museum, taking photos and chatting with members of the Knights of Lithuania and the Schuylkill County Lithuanian Women’s Club. Virbilas was not certain, but he thought his grandfather might have worked in Schuylkill County’s coal mines. The Lithuanian government presented its Merit for Lithuanians Worldwide medal to the Lithuanian Heritage Museum in Shenandoah in July. SUBMITTED PHOTO Cultural heritage The Knights of Lithuania Anthracite Council 144 sponsored a Lithuanian museum for many years at Annunciation BVM Catholic Church in Frackville. Several years ago, Anne Skirmantas approached the council with an offer to relocate the museum to the former Chaikowsky Funeral Home in Shenandoah. The funeral home, which was vacant, had been run by her parents, Leonard and Eleanor Chaikowsky. Through the efforts of Peter and Anne Skirmantas, the Knights council and volunteers, including the Chicago-based Sakyns (Roots) Lithuanian group, the archive was moved to the former funeral home at 318 E. Centre St. A repository of 150 years of Lithuanian culture in Schuylkill County, it opened in the fall of 2025. It honored the estimated 100,000 Lithuanians who left their homeland and settled in Pennsylvania’s anthracite region between 1865 and 1915. Lithuanian emigres brought their traditions with them, and built St. George Catholic Church in Shenandoah, the first Lithuanian Catholic church in America. The museum preserved stained glass windows from St. George’s and Our Lady of Siluva, a former Lithuanian parish in Maizeville. A sign bearing Lithuania’s national emblem marks the entrance to the Lithuanian Heritage Museum on Centre Street in Shenandoah. (AISHWARYA BEHL/STAFF PHOTO) A stained‑glass panel from St. George’s Lithuanian Catholic Church in Shenandoah, once the first and largest permanent Lithuanian parish in the United States, is displayed at the Lithuanian Heritage Museum. (AISHWARYA BEHL/STAFF PHOTO) A display highlights the Hill of Crosses in Šiauliai, Lithuania, a 19th‑century site of mourning that grew into a symbol of hope and national identity. (AISHWARYA BEHL/STAFF PHOTO) Show Caption 1 of 3 A sign bearing Lithuania’s national emblem marks the entrance to the Lithuanian Heritage Museum on Centre Street in Shenandoah. (AISHWARYA BEHL/STAFF PHOTO) Expand On display are woven tapestry, wood carvings, religious artifacts and family photos from five or so generations. There’s also a library of books in Lithuanian and English. A unique feature is a scale model of the Hill of Crosses, a shrine of more than 200,000 crosses and crucifixes in Lithuania. Testament to the nation’s faith, 100,000 worshippers turned out when Pope John Paul II celebrated Mass at the shrine in 1993. Anne served as curator of the museum for only eight months before her death, but she left an indelible mark on it. “She breathed new life into the museum,” Peter said. “She was very passionate about it.” Teacher, author, advocate Holder of a degree in theater production from Syracuse University, Anne Skirmantas taught at Los Angeles County High School for the Arts. She served as a stage and production manager for authors and Hollywood personalities, including Shenandoah native Darryl Ponicsan, an author and screenwriter. She wrote two books for Arcadia Press’ Images of America Series. “Shenandoah” was written for the town’s sesquicentennial. “Lithuanians of Schuylkill County” featured an extensive photo archive of the town. The late Anne Chaikowsky LaVoie Skirmantas was curator of the Lithuanian Heritage Museum in Shenandoah. (SUBMITTED PHOTO) In an effort to save it from the wrecking ball, she produced a DVD on St. George’s church. After it was razed in 2010, she co-authored “St. George Church: A Photographic Remembrance.” With Peter, to whom she was married for nine years, she made frequent trips to Lithuania. After receiving the medal, which Minister Budrys referred to as “Anne’s Award,” Peter revisited some of their favorite places in Vilnius. In a park, he saw a jogger wearing a shirt with the slogan “Everything’s going to be all right” on it. Those were the words Anne kept telling him when she was in hospice at St. Luke’s Hospital in Bethlehem. “Was it a coincidence or a message from her?” Peter asked. “I prefer to think of it as a message.” Share this: Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on X (Opens in new window) X Most Popular Most Popular Eviction: People moved from Hazleton woods where they had been living Eviction: People moved from Hazleton woods where they had been living Hazleton man gets decades in prison for child rape Hazleton man gets decades in prison for child rape Howard at Butler gets approval to build 192 apartments Howard at Butler gets approval to build 192 apartments Hazleton area court notes: Property transfers 9/12/26 Hazleton area court notes: Property transfers 9/12/26 Sword in the Stone Games opens second location in Laurel Mall Sword in the Stone Games opens second location in Laurel Mall Secrets: WVIA film gives glimpse at what miners left beneath Hazleton Secrets: WVIA film gives glimpse at what miners left beneath Hazleton HS FOOTBALL: Pocono Mountain West keeps Hazleton Area winless HS FOOTBALL: Pocono Mountain West keeps Hazleton Area winless ‘I really thought I was going to die:’ Barnesville man was on duty as NYC firefighter on 9/11 'I really thought I was going to die:' Barnesville man was on duty as NYC firefighter on 9/11 Bark alerts look for stressed-out Hazleton Area students Bark alerts look for stressed-out Hazleton Area students Michael Ferugio’s death on 9-11 remembered Friday in hometown Michael Ferugio's death on 9-11 remembered Friday in hometown More in Local News 2026 August 29

https://telex.hu/kulfold/2026/09/24/orba.text: Menü Kereső Orbán Balázs három dolgot döntött el egynapi EP-képviselőség után, az első, hogy levelet ír Külföld Fehér János Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Orbán Balázs a Fidesz képviselőjeként kedden kezdte meg a munkát az Európai Parlamentben , majd első napja után három dolog mellett határozta el magát, derült ki Facebook-posztjából . Orbán levélben akarja tájékoztatni az Európai Unió minden tagállamának parlamenti képviselőit, hogy mi történik Magyarországon. „Politikusokat tiltottak el a választáson való indulástól. Alkotmányos intézmények vezetőinek mandátumát szüntették meg. Hatóságokat küldtek az ellenzéki pártokra. Konzervatív intézeteket államosítottak és zártak be. Embereket zaklatnak folyamatosan hatósági eszközökkel, és olyan új hatóságot hoztak létre, amely példátlan jogosítványokat kapott, nincs fölötte érdemi kontroll, és deklarált célja a magyar cégek, vállalkozások zaklatása” – írta Orbán Balázs. „Sok minden kiderült azokról is, akik éveken keresztül demokráciából és jogállamiságból oktatták ki Magyarországot. Most, hogy hatalomra kerültek, kiderült, hogy ők nem mások, mint autoriter liberálisok, akik félnek az emberek haragjától, ezért az a legfontosabb céljuk, hogy a politikai versenyt kiiktassák” – folytatta az EP-képviselő. Azt állította, hogy nem panaszkodni mennek külföldre, még csak segítséget sem kérnek a magyar politikai küzdelmek megvívásához, de számítanak azok szolidaritására, akiknek még fontos a parlamentarizmus és a szabadság. Orbán Balázs egy kis lemaradásban van, mert párttársai, Deutsch Tamás és Gál Kinga már két héttel ezelőtt írtak az EP-képviselőknek, hogy szerintük Magyarországon önkényuralmi rendszer kiépítése zajlik, és felszámolják a demokráciát. Orbán Balázs második vállalása, hogy utánajár az Európai Parlament által megrendelt közvélemény-kutatásoknak, míg harmadik ígérete szerint egy olyan kutatást kér az EP kutatószolgálatáról, ami arra ad választ, hogy milyen szerepet játszik a genderpolitika az EU külpolitikájában. A fideszes politikus Szekeres Pál EP-mandátumát kapta meg , aki hétfőn tett esküt a magyar Országgyűlés előtt. Photograph: Pascal Rossignol/Reuters France French court jails six men for manslaughter over mass drowning in Channel Seven others found guilty of lesser charges in connection to incident in 2021 when inflatable dinghy sank killing at least 27 people with four more still missing Angelique Chrisafis in Paris Wed 30 Sep 2026 11.58 EDT Last modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 12.27 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A Paris court has jailed six ⁠men for manslaughter over the deaths of at least 27 people in the worst mass drowning on record from a small-boat crossing in the Channel. Seven other men were ⁠found guilty of lesser smuggling charges with varying degrees of seriousness, including facilitating illegal immigration as part of ⁠an organised gang and criminal conspiracy. Five years on, another four people are still missing. The court heard that the sinking of an inflatable dinghy in November 2021 was caused by “individuals driven by greed, with utter disregard for human life”. Prosecutors said the convicted men helped launch a “substandard small boat, uncertified, unfit for navigation on the open sea, overcrowded and lacking appropriate lifejackets”. Emmanuel Daoud, a lawyer for one victim’s family, called the proceedings a “trial of greed, cynicism and inhumanity”. Twenty-seven people were confirmed dead when their inflatable dinghy sank in the early hours of 24 November 2021. Four people remain unaccounted for. View image in fullscreen Lawyers and relatives of victims arrive at court in Paris for the trial of the alleged smugglers. Photograph: Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP/Getty Images The victims were mostly Iraqi Kurds, but also included people who were Afghan, Ethiopian, Iranian, Somali, Vietnamese and Egyptian. The youngest known victim was a seven-year-old girl. The confirmed dead included 15 men, seven women and two teenagers. Sentences for the six men found guilty of manslaughter ranged ‌from six to 10 years in prison. For others, sentences ranged from six months suspended to four ​years in prison. The court heard that the men were linked to Afghan and Iraqi-Kurdish smuggling networks ⁠that organised the migrants’ passage to Britain from camps near Grande-Synthe and Calais in northern France . One man was found innocent. According to testimony from the two survivors, the flimsy boat, which had attempted to cross one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes between the northern French coast and Kent in southern England began to deflate and take on water after several hours at sea. Passengers fell overboard and drowned one after another, despite making about a dozen desperate calls for help to French and British rescue services. Only two men survived. For the people onboard the sinking boat, despite several distress calls, it was nearly 12 hours after the first pleas for help before the dinghy was finally found by a French fishing vessel. A separate investigation is continuing in France into seven French military personnel – five members at a maritime rescue coordination centre, and two sailors onboard a patrol vessel. They have been under investigation since 2023 for failing to help a person in danger. They deny the allegations. Zana Mahmand Mohammed travelled from Erbil in Iraqi Kurdistan to address the court about his younger brother, Twana, 18, who drowned in the disaster but whose body has never been found. He said: “We’ve been waiting for our brother’s body for five years. I live with the uncertainty of ever finding out what happened. We lost a member of our family. He had a project for another future to live … ” The family had tried to dissuade Twana from leaving home, but he had wanted to find a job and develop his sporting success as a black belt in taekwondo and escape the violence and insecurity of his region. Mohammed said every time he read in the media about other small boats in difficulty, he relived the tragedy. “Destruction is being repeated,” he said.
